title: How Will The Custom HBM Business Work?
gist: HBM4 introduces a customizable base die, opening a new custom-memory business largely reserved for hyperscalers and design-savvy fabless players like Marvell, while memory makers themselves are stepping back from doing the custom design work due to resource constraints.

insights.claim: Starting with HBM4, the base (logic) die of an HBM stack has moved from a DRAM process to a modern finFET logic process (likely 4nm or beyond), meaning a logic foundry rather than the memory maker now manufactures it even for the standard configuration.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: This process split is what structurally enables custom base-die designs; investors should watch logic foundries (TSMC, Samsung Foundry, Intel Foundry) gaining a new HBM-adjacent revenue stream previously captured entirely by memory makers.
insights.quote: For power and performance, they moved to logic processes.

insights.claim: HBM4 and its successors allow the standard base die to be swapped for a customized one that handles specific AI workloads more efficiently, while the memory layers themselves remain uncustomized.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Differentiation in AI accelerators is shifting from pure compute-die design to the compute-memory interface, a new axis of competitive advantage for XPU vendors.

insights.claim: Custom HBM is effectively restricted to hyperscalers because they can fund a chip-design project, run large fleets dedicated to narrow AI workload types (unlike general-purpose web servers), and cannot wait for JEDEC's slower standardization pace to match the speed of AI compute evolution.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Custom HBM is a moat available only to the largest AI compute buyers, reinforcing hyperscaler advantage over smaller cloud/AI infrastructure players who must rely on standard, allocation-constrained HBM.
insights.quote: How to customize those HBM base dies based on their workload?

insights.claim: Enterprise (non-hyperscaler) customers are beginning to explore building their own XPUs and by extension custom memory, but per Marvell this is still in an early evaluation phase.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Watch for a second wave of custom-silicon demand beyond the hyperscalers (Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta) as enterprises look to reduce dependence on merchant GPU/accelerator supply.
insights.quote: We started to see more and more that enterprise customers are also trying to build their own XPUs,

insights.claim: Marvell has built a custom cloud computing division to design custom XPUs for hyperscaler clients and, in order to reduce design effort, is trying to build a single custom HBM offering that can serve multiple different customer XPU interfaces.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Marvell is positioning itself as a horizontal custom-silicon/custom-memory integrator for hyperscalers, a business model investors should track as a proxy for hyperscaler custom-silicon capex.
insights.quote: We are trying to see what the different customer requirements are and how to navigate through a single HBM offering and address those multiple customers,

themes.theme: Technical and cost mechanics of customization

insights.claim: Moving the memory controller from the host XPU die into the custom HBM base die removes the memory PHY (about 70% smaller than a standard DRAM PHY) from the compute die, freeing roughly 25% more area for compute capability while reducing power and increasing overall XPU efficiency.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: This is a concrete, quantified performance/power benefit that makes cHBM economically attractive even before considering interface differentiation, supporting continued hyperscaler investment in custom silicon programs.
insights.quote: That is around 70% smaller than a standard DRAM PHY. It enables 25% more compute capabilities on the compute die. It reduces the overall power, and it increases the efficiency of the whole XPU die.

insights.claim: Because the custom base die adds cost only on a cheaper logic process while removing controller area from the more expensive leading-edge host die, the net effect of moving the controller to the base die is a cost win for the XPU vendor.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: cHBM is not merely a performance play but a die-cost optimization lever, which strengthens the economic case for hyperscalers to keep investing in custom base-die programs even amid tight memory supply.

insights.claim: A larger die shoreline created by removing the PHY from the compute die lets an XPU connect to more HBM stacks, increasing total memory capacity per compute tile.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Custom HBM designs could let AI accelerators pack more memory bandwidth/capacity per chip than standard HBM designs, a potential competitive edge in memory-bound AI inference workloads.

themes.theme: Who does the design, manufacturing, and assembly work

insights.claim: Design is the hardest and most resource-constrained of the four steps (design, manufacturing/wafer test, assembly, final test) in a custom HBM project, and memory makers themselves are reluctant to take on custom base-die design work because they lack spare design teams.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Design capacity, not manufacturing capacity, is the real bottleneck for custom HBM growth, favoring fabless design specialists (Marvell) and hyperscalers with in-house silicon teams over traditional memory makers as the primary suppliers of cHBM.
insights.quote: But memory companies need to do the design and manufacturing [of custom HBM], and we are resource-constrained.

insights.claim: There is no single business model for who owns stack assembly in custom HBM projects: ownership of design and integration is negotiated per project between the memory house, logic foundry, and assembly facility, with some hyperscaler customers taking full ownership themselves.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: The custom HBM supply chain is fragmenting into bespoke, negotiated partnerships rather than a standardized industry structure, creating both risk (execution complexity) and opportunity (higher-margin integration services) for capable players.
insights.quote: Some customers give full ownership of the logic to the guys designing it while taking full ownership of the integration.

insights.claim: TSMC is working with Winbond, where Winbond supplies memory wafers and TSMC assembles the stack, a deal reported as taking pressure off the other three main memory makers (Micron, Samsung, SK Hynix).
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: A foundry-led HBM supply chain (TSMC plus a secondary memory supplier like Winbond) is emerging as an alternative to the traditional Big 3 memory maker oligopoly, a potential new competitive vector in HBM supply.

insights.claim: As an alternative to true HBM stacks, some designs are stacking up to four standard DRAM dies directly atop a logic host using hybrid bonding, a technique already in production for DRAM-on-logic even though HBM itself still uses microbumps.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: This stacked-DRAM-on-logic approach is a lower-cost, faster-to-market substitute for true HBM that could relieve pressure on HBM allocation for some AI workloads, though Synopsys expects fewer than 20 such projects per year.
insights.quote: In designs that have already taped out, the bottom logic die is flipped face up and hybrid bonds connect to the downward-facing DRAM wafer on top,

insights.claim: The primary motivation for stacking standard DRAM on logic via hybrid bonding is not just working around HBM supply shortages but achieving significantly lower latency and lower power than HBM, because of the tight bond pitch versus HBM's microbumps.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: This reframes stacked-DRAM-on-logic as a genuine performance alternative rather than a stopgap, meaning demand for it may persist even after HBM supply loosens.
insights.quote: An application-level reason is that it gets you significantly lower latency because now you’re using hybrid bonds or bumps that are tightly spaced to do the transfer — and lower power as well.

insights.claim: Memory suppliers have reportedly sold out their fabs for the next one and a half to two years amid a huge memory shortage and skyrocketing prices, even as custom HBM demand is layered on top.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: A multi-year memory supply crunch is a structural tailwind for memory maker pricing power (Micron, Samsung, SK Hynix) and a constraint investors should model into AI hardware cost and margin forecasts through at least 2028.
insights.quote: There is a huge shortage of memory, and prices are skyrocketing,

insights.claim: Custom HBM demand is not expected to add to total memory capacity strain because industry memory requirements don't distinguish standard from custom units; instead, custom HBM changes the mix of what capacity is used for, potentially complicating supply forecasting.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Investors modeling HBM supply/demand should treat cHBM as a mix-shift risk rather than an incremental-demand risk, but should expect more forecasting uncertainty as customization spreads across more foundry/assembly partners.

insights.claim: With custom HBM projects already underway, custom HBM stacks are expected to begin reaching datacenters within roughly one to two years of this article's publication.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Investors should watch for commercial custom HBM deployments (from Marvell-designed XPUs and similar programs) landing in hyperscaler datacenters around 2027-2028.
insights.quote: With projects underway now, custom HBM stacks should be hitting datacenters in a year, or maybe two.
